items.excerpt: Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Thursday, including US President Donald Trump saying Washington is not negotiating with Iran and that "something one way or the other” will happen “fairly soon," Türkiye, Qatar, Indonesia and Pakistan signing a new defense cooperation pact, an attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport killing 1 and injuring 8, and Russia releasing a 73-year-old American who was imprisoned for fighting alongside Ukrainian forces. US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Iran, adding that “something one way or the other” will happen “fairly soon.” “No, I think we’re not negotiating,” Trump told reporters upon returning from a rally in South Carolina. “We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon.”

items.title: Early Edition: October 22, 2026
items.excerpt: A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news: IRAN WAR Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy today said four vessels involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were simultaneously hit and caught fire after being tracked by Iranian forces yesterday. The IRGC added that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned the U.S. military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. Tala Ramadan reports for Reuters. The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the U.S. midterms, U.S. officials and other sources told the New York Times. The countries’ militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers. The strikes would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Julian E. Barnes, Eric Schmitt, Farnaz Fassihi, Natan Odenheimer, and Ronen Bergman report. Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets on Monday conducted a sortie, flying as far as the Iranian border, Israeli and U.S. officials told Axios. The operation took place on the same day U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but wasn’t connected to Hegseth’s visit. Barak Ravid reports. IRAN WAR – YEMEN Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation yesterday blamed the Iran-aligned Houthis for a new attack on the eastern Saudi city of Dammam’s airport which killed two people and injured another eight. The U.S. State Department said it ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their families from the kingdom in response to increased hostilities against Saudi Arabia by the Houthis. David Gritten reports for BBC News; James T. Areddy and Abeer Ayyoub report for the Wall Street Journal. IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS ... New York Democrat congressional candidate Brad Lander yesterday said he was briefly detained and released by the Israeli military while he was supporting Palestinian farmers during an olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. The New Israel Fund said approximately 90 volunteers of what they’re calling the Protect the Harvest initiative were released. Two Israeli lawyers told NPR it was the largest mass detention of activists in the occupied West Bank in at least a decade. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said Lander’s actions amounted to “political provocation,” and noted that he chose to enter a restricted area and participate in an unauthorized activity without coordinating with local authorities. Joseph De Avila reports for the Wall Street Journal; Ruth Sherlock, Samantha Balaban, Nuha Musleh, and Daniel Estrin report. RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff yesterday called Russian President Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” following the release of U.S. citizen Stephen James Hubbard from Russian custody. In a meeting between the pair, Putin told Witkoff that he “agrees in principle” to resuming trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States to end the war in Ukraine, Russian and U.S. officials told Axios. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he hoped the three-way talks will be held as soon as possible, preferably no later than early November. David E. Sanger, Kim Barker, and Ivan Nechepurenko report for the New York Times; Barak Ravid reports; Ron Popeski reports for Reuters. Ukraine’s Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko yesterday said a Russian missile attack was launched at Ukraine’s capital, injuring six people. The attack came hours after Putin said he was “ready in principle” to resume peace talks and after Trump said the world was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards its capital Moscow overnight. Jaroslav Lukiv reports for BBC News; Olena Harmash and Gleb Bryanski report for Reuters. ... The U.N. World Meteorological Organization yesterday said the El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels across the world like a “wrecking ball,” causing floods and droughts. The WMO’s seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong and cause temperatures to rise by 3.8 degrees Celsius. WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said “we have not seen in our records 3.8. We have seen around 3 in some record El Niños before, with very substantive impacts across the world.” Olivia Le Poidevin reports for Reuters. ... New Mexico yesterday filed a civil lawsuit against sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime lawyer and accountant, Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn, accusing the pair of helping finance and conceal Epstein’s sex trafficking at his remote Zorro Ranch property in Stanley, New Mexico. The suit alleges several Jane Does, including minors, were abused at the ranch, and Indyke arranged payments to victims that left them indebted to Epstein, while Kahn monitored the spending of victims and even prepared tax returns for some. Khadeeja Safdar reports for the Wall Street Journal. A New Mexico judge yesterday ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties after a jury in September found that the company misled users about their data privacy. The penalties come nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal first broke. New Mexico is the only state to take its claims to trial after 48 others settled with Meta. Josephine Walker reports for Axios.

items.excerpt: ## Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Iran's government says seven oil tankers have caught fire or been damaged in the strategic Strait of Hormuz. This comes amid rising tensions over the prospect of a return to all-out war. Iranian state television cites the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy which threatens to strike U.S. military bases if the United States continues guiding commercial ships through the strait. The U.S. is meanwhile sending more military assets to the region. Mediators are trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to talks. Iran has proposed ending the conflict if the U.S. meets certain conditions. But U.S. President Donald Trump rejected it although discussions have continued. ## Russian missiles pound Kyiv as Moscow says over 800 Ukrainian drones downed KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia has launched a nighttime missile barrage on Kyiv while its military says it intercepted more than 800 Ukrainian drones targeting Moscow and other Russian cities. The attacks dampen hopes for peace talks. Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed “in principle” to resume negotiations with Ukraine and the U.S. but no date is set. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday reported deadly attacks across 12 regions with Kyiv enduring significant damage. Ukraine is bracing for winter as Russia targets its power grid. A U.S. envoy faced criticism for flattering Putin which highlights ongoing tensions and challenges in reaching a resolution. ## Iran says 7 tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, and other Mideast news Iran's state television reports that seven oil tankers have been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz. This happened overnight Thursday, possibly marking the largest single-day incident since the Iran war began on February 28. Four tankers caught fire after being targeted, while three others were immobilized by naval mines. The report warns that the Revolutionary Guard may target U.S. bases if the U.S. tries to allow tankers to transit through other parts of the strait. Meanwhile, Yemen’s Defense Ministry warns that Houthi rallies could be targeted, and Saudi Arabia reports two deaths from an attack on King Fahd International Airport. ## Deportations climb under Trump but fall short of White House target, a ... ## AI stocks tumble and drag down markets worldwide as oil prices climb NEW YORK (AP) — AI stocks are tumbling and dragging stock markets down around the world. The S&P 500 sank 0.8% Thursday following even sharper losses in Asia, whose markets are full of AI and other technology stocks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 132 points, and the Nasdaq composite fell 1.3%. AI stocks have been shaky recently on worries that their boom may be under threat because of high interest rates. Also weighing on markets worldwide is a jump in oil prices. The price of Brent crude oil touched its highest level since May because of worries about the war with Iran.

items.title: IIF Global Macro Views: What the Breadth of U.S. Inflation Signals > The Institute of International Finance
items.excerpt: - Broad inflation is the Fed’s challenge; entrenchment is the risk. Prices are rising across much of the U.S. economy, but softer momentum and weaker hiring complicate the case for further tightening. - The latest price shock is being transmitted through production costs. Energy pushed September CPI and PPI higher, while measures of underlying inflation rose more moderately. - Households are more alarmed about inflation than bond investors. Fuel prices shift near-term expectations quickly; evidence that breadth changes longer-term beliefs is less conclusive. - Monetary policy is the clearest link to bond yields. Persistent breadth could raise the expected policy path, although real yields also respond to fiscal, investment, and global forces.

items.title: US inflation rose slightly last month after 2 years of steady cooling but remained low
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — Inflation in the United States ticked up in October, driven by costlier rents, used cars and air fares, a sign that price increases might be leveling off after having slowed in September to their lowest pace since 2021. ... Consumer prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 2.4% in September. It was the first rise in annual inflation in seven months. From September to October, prices edged up 0.2%, the same as the previous month. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, “core” prices rose 3.3% from a year earlier, the same as in September. From September to October, core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Over the long run, core inflation at that pace would exceed the Fed’s 2% target. ... An uptick in prices, if sustained, could stir concerns in financial markets that progress in taming inflation may be slowing. It might also make the Federal Reserve less inclined to cut its key interest rate in the coming months, as its officials have previously indicated they likely would. ... Still, most economists think inflation will eventually resume its slowdown. Consumer inflation, which peaked at 9.1% in 2022, has since fallen steadily, though overall prices are still about 20% higher than they were three years ago. ... In addition, the economy is growing faster than many economists had expected earlier this year. It has expanded at nearly a 3% annual rate over the past six months, with consumers, particularly those with higher incomes, spending freely and fueling growth. ... A survey released Tuesday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that consumers expect prices to rise just 2.9% in the next 12 months, which would be the lowest such measure in nearly four years. Lower inflation expectations are important because when consumers expect milder price increases, they’re less likely to act in ways that raise inflation, such as accelerating their purchases or demanding higher pay to offset higher prices. ... Another potential source of relief for Americans’ budgets is in apartment rents. They are now barely rising on average nationwide, according to the real estate brokerage Redfin. Its measure of median rent was just 0.2% higher than it was a year ago in October, at $1,619, though that figure reflects rents only for new leases.

items.excerpt: U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the United States would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold onto recent gains. The S&P 500 was down 1.4% by midmorning, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq saw declines of 2.2%. The price of international Brent crude climbed more than 2%, while U.S. crude gained more than 1%. ... Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the last several months — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets as riskier ones like tech stocks sold off. That sent bond yields lower. ... The broad sell-off was sparked in part by reporting Wednesday that Israel and the U.S. were preparing for a military operation in Iran after the November midterm elections. ... The slide in the Nasdaq got additional fuel Thursday morning after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an appearance on CNBC that capital to finance the AI investment boom was becoming “scarce” due to higher interest rates and a glut of existing spending commitments.

It follows Thomas, played by Hanns Zischler, and his daughter, played by Sandra Hüller, on a trip from West Germany to East Germany after many years away. In her review, Associated Press Film Writer Lindsey Bahr writes that Pawlikowski's film is painterly and profound, a brisk and somber indictment of the idea of postwar optimism that fits neatly in his unofficial trilogy with “Ida” and “Cold War.” “Fatherland” opens in select theaters Friday. Kathleen Kennedy, chair of AFI's board, praised Cruise as a global icon and highlighted his dedication to film. Tom Rhys Harries stars as Matt Hagen, a rising actor whose life changes after a mobster disfigures him. He turns to a scientist, played by Naomi Ackie, for help.
